chunks.title: Rule of Thirds
chunks.content: The rule of thirds divides the picture plane into a 3x3 grid by placing two equally spaced horizontal lines and two equally spaced vertical lines. The four intersections of these lines are the conventional anchor points where the eye naturally settles. In oil painting, placing a primary focal mass at or near one of these intersections produces a composition that reads as composed rather than centered. A centered subject tends to feel static; an off-axis subject gains directional energy. The rule does not require literal intersection placement: a powerful alternative is to align a strong edge of the subject with a third-line, which gives the figure breathing room and gives the negative space its own weight. For panoramic landscapes, the lower third-line often holds the horizon, leaving the upper two-thirds open to sky. For portrait work, the eyes typically sit on the upper third-line. When prompting a reference generator, name the off-axis placement explicitly and describe which third-line anchors the focal mass.

chunks.title: Golden Ratio and Fibonacci Spiral
chunks.content: The golden ratio, approximately 1:1.618, organizes composition through a logarithmic spiral that thickens by the same proportion with each quarter-turn. In oil painting this guides the eye along a curving path from a foreground corner into the focal mass and onward into the background. The spiral is not a literal overlay; it is a device for confirming that the dominant diagonal of a composition follows a self-similar curve rather than a straight slash. Painters such as Vermeer in Girl with a Pearl Earring and Seurat in A Sunday Afternoon place key masses along this curve. Practical use: divide the canvas into a golden rectangle, subdivide into a square and a smaller golden rectangle, repeat to locate the spiral's growth points. A subject at the spiral's tight inner curl reads as the resolved end of the viewer's journey. When prompting a reference generator, name the spiral's anchor and direction; do not name both the rule and the supporting geometry.

chunks.title: Focal Hierarchy and Dominance
chunks.content: Focal hierarchy is the deliberate ordering of visual weights so the eye arrives at one primary destination, then visits secondary and tertiary points in a controlled sequence. Dominance is established by contrast: high-value light against deep shadow, saturated complementary against muted analogous color, sharp edge against soft lost edges, or large mass against small accents. A single dominant focal point should always exist; secondary points should reinforce, not compete with, the primary. In oil painting, dominance is rarely achieved by one variable alone. A focal area is typically the convergence of three or four: brightest light, warmest hue, sharpest edge, highest chroma. When two focal points are equally weighted, the result reads as indecisive. Use value to do the heavy lifting; chroma and edge quality are then applied as reinforcement. Squint at the canvas to verify that the value map alone resolves the hierarchy without color. When prompting a reference generator, name the hierarchy in order — primary, secondary, tertiary — and specify the contrast type.

chunks.title: Atmospheric Perspective
chunks.content: Atmospheric perspective, also called aerial perspective, is the optical phenomenon by which distant objects lose value contrast, chroma, and edge sharpness as a function of the air mass between them and the viewer. In oil painting this is rendered by pushing distant planes toward a unified middle-value gray-blue, reducing the temperature contrast between local color and the surrounding atmosphere, and softening edges until they dissolve into adjacent tones. The most reliable cue is value contrast: a foreground tree shows near-black shadow against near-white light, while a distant tree of the same species narrows to two or four values within a compressed middle range. Chroma falls off along a curve: distant reds become dusty roses, distant greens shift toward Payne's gray with viridian undertones. The painter should preserve at least one crisp edge per plane transition to keep the depth readable. When prompting a reference generator, name the depth plane and specify which value range, chroma level, and edge quality apply.

chunks.title: Leading Lines
chunks.content: Leading lines are linear or implied-linear elements that direct the eye toward a focal point or along a predetermined path through the picture. They may be actual edges — a shoreline, a fence, a road, an arm — or they may be constructed from repeated marks, value transitions, or chromatic rhythm. Strong leading lines typically begin at a corner or edge of the canvas, never at the center, and travel on a diagonal or gentle curve rather than a vertical or horizontal, because diagonals carry momentum. Lines that point directly at the center read as trivial; lines that point slightly off-center and then resolve into a focal mass read as composed. Converging lines exaggerate depth; divergent or radiating lines exaggerate drama. The painter should also manage counter-lines, secondary diagonals that oppose the primary, to add tension and prevent monotony. A line that exits the canvas should exit cleanly at a corner or a third, not at the midpoint of an edge. When prompting a reference generator, name the line type and its terminus.

chunks.title: Negative Space
chunks.content: Negative space is the area of the canvas not taken up by the primary subject: the sky around a figure, the wall behind a still life, the water between boats. In oil painting, negative space is treated as active shape rather than leftover area, and its contours are as carefully drawn as the subject's. The contour where subject meets negative space is one of the most powerful edges in the picture. Squinting reveals the negative shapes as abstract silhouettes; if a silhouette is uninteresting, the composition will be uninteresting regardless of subject detail. Good negative space carries its own internal value structure, a designed pattern of lights and darks that balances the subject's pattern. A common mistake is to fill negative space with detail, texture, or incidental objects in the belief that emptiness is unfinished; in fact, confident restraint is what gives the focal subject room to operate. When prompting a reference generator, name the dominant negative shape and describe its contour.

chunks.title: Gestural Composition
chunks.content: Gestural composition refers to arranging the major masses and directional movements of a picture before any detail is committed, working from the largest energy vectors down to the smallest marks. In oil painting this typically begins with a thumbnail or a small alla prima sketch that resolves only the major value masses, the dominant angles, and the implied movement from one side of the canvas to the other. The composition is felt as a whole before it is described piece by piece. Every painter has a gestural instinct; the goal of disciplined gestural composition is to make that instinct conscious and revisable. Common failures include starting at the focal point and building outward, which produces a tight center and a weak surround, or starting with detail, which produces an incoherent overall read. A useful test: the painting should be legible at thumbnail size, then at one-third size, then at full size, with each step adding resolution without changing the gestural structure. When prompting a reference generator, name the dominant gestural vector and the two largest masses.

chunks.title: Value Structure and Notan
chunks.content: Notan is the Japanese design principle of arranging light and dark masses into a clear two- or three-value structure independent of color and detail. In oil painting, notan is established before color and is the single most reliable predictor of whether a finished picture will feel composed. The painter makes a thumbnail in two values, typically a light and a dark, that resolves the entire composition. If the notan thumbnail is incoherent, no color will rescue it; if the notan is strong, color becomes a vehicle for refinement rather than rescue. Value structure is usually described in three to five planes: deepest shadow, mid-shadow, mid-light, light, and highest light. The dominant value, the one that occupies the largest area, sets the key of the painting and determines whether the overall mood reads as high-key, middle-key, or low-key. A common error is to distribute values evenly, producing a flat, freckled read; another is to alternate light-dark-light-dark in stripes, producing a fence-like rhythm. When prompting a reference generator, name the value key and the dominant value mass.

chunks.title: Edge Control and Lost and Found
chunks.content: Edge control is the deliberate variation of contour sharpness across the picture to direct attention and to model form. Hard edges advance toward the viewer and invite close reading; soft edges recede and invite peripheral reading; lost edges dissolve one form into its neighbor and create atmospheric or rhythmic continuity. The lost-and-found principle states that an edge should rarely be uniformly hard or uniformly soft across its length; instead, segments of crisp contour should alternate with segments that fade or are absorbed. A face might have a crisp edge along the jaw into the background and a lost edge where the hair meets the shadow; a still-life fruit might have a hard edge at its terminator and a lost edge where it tucks behind a cloth. The painter manages edges by brush pressure, medium loading, and the wetness of the surrounding paint. When prompting a reference generator, name the edge quality per major contour — hard, soft, or lost — and the contour's role.

chunks.title: Framing and Crop
chunks.content: Framing and crop determine how much of the implied world the painter admits into the rectangle and how that rectangle is bounded. A tight crop flattens depth and forces intimacy with the subject; a wide crop expands depth and pulls the viewer into a larger narrative. The crop also defines the relationship of the subject to its boundaries: a figure touching all four edges feels trapped; a figure breathing off all four edges feels lost; a figure comfortably weighted to two or three edges with one or two edges open feels composed. In oil painting the crop is rarely the same as the photographer's crop; the painter actively chooses which elements to include, exclude, or shift. The four corners of the canvas are particularly important because the eye returns to them during viewing, and a stray highlight or a poorly placed mass in a corner will pull the composition apart. When prompting a reference generator, name the crop ratio and which edges the subject approaches.
